You use two conjoined sentences as conditionals. One of these sentences represents a condition needed (“if clause”) to influence or generate the second action (“result clause”).

Zero conditional is used when you want to express only true facts and true results, while the first conditional implies a probability because you use it when you talk about things that might happen in the future. 

Remember, the first conditional describes a particular situation while the zero conditional describes what happens in general, for example:

Zero Conditional

  • If you add an HTML codes, it compiles all the data.

First Conditional

  • If binary protocols come back, the internet of things will generate more data than ever.

You use will when you want to express expectations and hopes in regards to the future.

You use will as a future tense form to express a probable situation that might happen in the future. Also, when you make fast decisions and predictions based on our opinions; when you make promises or offers, and for predictable behaviors. Let’s see some examples:

  • Building more binary protocols will represent an advance in technology.
  • Once you understand the representational state transfer (REST) you will identify the simple object access protocol SOAP.

Remember that you use the verb in base form after the auxiliary will to from the future tense.

  • Language programming will use binary codes.
  • Developers will enhance codes for programming.

Subordination is part of the efficiency of language to make more complex sentences. It makes part of the process of joining sentences with related ideas.

In writing, subordination is the process of putting together short, brief sentences with similar ideas into a longer sentence.

To make this process you use dependent words, such as: after, although, because or when, among others. Then, in front of one independent sentence that finally, it becomes a dependent clause and it is not a complete sentence anymore

David: Hey, Frank! How's it going?
Frank: Good, thanks. But, I'm a little bit worried because I'll publish in this magazine about the future of language programming. So, I‘m reading about it to know more and do a great job.
David: I see. Let's talk about it then. What does it say?
Frank: It states that if programming developers rely on REST's simplicity, it will enhance the communications at a constant rate between producers and consumers. So, REST will prevail among others protocols.
David: I know REST is preferred over other protocol styles because it does not leverage too much bandwidth, which makes it an appropriate fit to work on the internet.

Frank: Programmers think that if they send bytes directly to the parsing process, it will be faster. This is really an upcoming change for programming innovations. Then, if JSON packets and REST provide such tighter encoding, the old world of XML data slightly disappears.
David: Wow! I will summarize this on my notepad because I think we need it as a future reference, don't you think?
Frank: Please. Also, the famous HTML5 will also open the possibilities to present video clips with HTML codes in the future.
David: What about smartphones? If we want to get real-time conditions of the roads, we simply use the Waze® app. As databases extent facilities, people will get information about the location and the source of any disturbance on the street much faster.

David: According to that rate of change, if language programming continues with such development, what will be its key features?
Frank: The innumerable programming dialects are those key features that need to be translated for a browser or the Node.js to understand them; thus transcoding robots will appear to do it automatically. Additionally, PHP will prevail for a longer period if only contributes to avoiding legal apps to be rewritten.
David: In conclusion, I would say ordinary people will eventually need to deal with APIs because an entire social system may have to communicate with thousands of code lines at the speed of light.
